q: A patient with mitral stenosis develops fast AF and becomes breathless. Why does tachycardia cause decompensation?
o: It shortens diastole, reducing filling across the stenotic valve
why: MS is a fixed cardiac output state. Tachycardia shortens diastolic filling time, raising LA pressure and causing pulmonary oedema. Control the rate.

q: Which is the most common cause of mitral stenosis?
why: Rheumatic heart disease is the commonest cause; patients often present in AF. Dyspnoea does not always match the severity of stenosis.

q: Three days after an inferior MI, a patient develops acute severe mitral regurgitation. Which papillary muscle has most likely ruptured, and why?
o: Anterolateral; single supply from the RCA
Posteromedial; single supply from the RCA
Anterolateral; dual supply from LAD and LCx
Posteromedial; dual supply from LAD and LCx
Neither: papillary muscles do not rupture
why: The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply (usually from the RCA), so it is vulnerable after inferior MI. The anterolateral muscle has a dual supply (LAD/LCx).

q: On TOE, which finding indicates severe mitral regurgitation?
o: Vena contracta ≥0.7 cm or a central jet over 40% of LA area
why: Severe MR: vena contracta ≥0.7 cm, central jet over 40% of LA area (over 10 cm²), regurgitant volume ≥60 ml, regurgitant fraction ≥50% or EROA ≥0.4 cm²; also assess PA pressure.

q: Why is TOE performed before cardioversion in a patient with AF for more than 48 hours who is not anticoagulated?
o: To check the oesophagus for varices
why: Thrombus can form in the LA appendage after 48 hours of AF; cardioversion could dislodge it and cause a stroke.

q: What is the most appropriate anaesthetic approach for an elective TOE-guided cardioversion?
o: Short-acting rapid-onset agent, fasted patient, full monitoring
why: An elective cardioversion is a short procedure: fasted, full AAGBI monitoring, a rapid-onset short-acting agent (e.g. propofol), pads applied before induction.

q: Cardioversion fails after three synchronised biphasic shocks in an unstable patient. What is the next step?
o: Amiodarone 300 mg IV, then repeat the shock
why: After up to three failed shocks, give amiodarone 300 mg IV (loading) and repeat the shock.

q: A patient with a pacemaker develops low cardiac output after their device was set to VVI pacing. What is the likely problem?
o: Pacemaker syndrome from loss of AV synchrony
why: Pacemaker syndrome is loss of AV synchrony with reduced cardiac output; it is treated by switching to a dual-chamber (DDD) mode.

q: Which is an indication for a permanent pacemaker?
why: Indications include 2:1 and third-degree AV block, alternating bundle branch block, syncope with bifascicular block and symptomatic sinus node disease.

q: What is the term for a pacemaker’s ability to detect intrinsic cardiac activity?
why: Sensitivity is the ability to detect intrinsic activity; capture is successful depolarisation of the myocardium after a pacing stimulus.
